title: Van Cortlandt Park — Stockbridge Memorial
summary: At Indian Field, the Chief Nimham Memorial remembers Native soldiers killed fighting for the American cause on August 31, 1778. David Bunn Martine’s painting connects that history with possible Shinnecock and Montaukett participation.
address_label: Chief Nimham Memorial, Van Cortlandt Park East near East 238th Street / Oneida Avenue, Bronx, NY
map_geometry_source: ParkMagnet, Van Cortlandt Park, named Chief Nimham Memorial point: 40.89930864, -73.87352933; cross-checked against Historic Districts Council’s street location, September 11, 2026.
why_this_matters: The memorial connects the American Revolution to Native soldiers whose families also fought to hold on to their homelands. David Bunn Martine’s painting carries this remembrance into Long Island’s contemporary Native art, inviting attention to people whose individual stories are still being recovered.
introduction_title: Native soldiers in the American Revolution
introduction_content:
On the eastern edge of Van Cortlandt Park, a bronze plaque set into a stone memorial remembers Native soldiers who died in the Revolutionary War. The Chief Nimham Memorial stands at Indian Field, near Van Cortlandt Park East and East 238th Street.[6]

The Stockbridge company included Mohican, Wappinger, and Munsee men. Fighting alongside the Americans also offered a way to defend their own communities and homelands. Wappinger leader Daniel Nimham had already carried a struggle for land rights to England; he and his son Abraham later served in the Continental Army.[1]
oral_history_title: David Bunn Martine: remembering a possible Long Island soldier
oral_history_content:
Martine imagines a Shinnecock/Montaukett member of the company in a quiet moment beside the water. Ma’s House describes the painting as a conjectural reconstruction and raises the possibility that men from those Long Island communities also served. Clothing details draw on Johann von Ewald’s eyewitness depiction of a Stockbridge soldier.[4]

The painting brings that possible connection into view; the identity of an individual Shinnecock or Montaukett casualty remains unconfirmed. The artwork retains “ca. 1777” in its title; the battle commemorated here occurred in 1778.[4][1]

See the exhibition post, explore Martine’s work, or continue to Ma’s House on the Shinnecock Reservation.
history_content:
August 31, 1778: the Battle of Kingsbridge

While operating near Van Cortlandt’s Ridge, roughly sixty Stockbridge soldiers encountered a much larger British force. Queen’s Rangers and mounted troops outflanked them. Fighting continued as the men tried to withdraw through the woods.[2]

Daniel and Abraham Nimham were among those killed. Accounts differ on the losses: the National Park Service reports estimates ranging from fifteen to forty Native dead. The battle is also remembered as the Stockbridge Massacre.[1][2]

Read the memorial

August 31, 1778 upon this field Chief Nimham and seventeen Stockbridge Indians as allies of the Patriots gave their lives for liberty.

The plaque’s commemorative count is smaller than some estimates for the battle as a whole. Dedicated on June 14, 1906, the memorial was restored by NYC Parks’ monuments conservation program in summer 2016.[3]

Service, land, and survival

Military service did not protect the Stockbridge community from dispossession. After the Revolution, land pressures helped force families westward. The Stockbridge-Munsee Community continues today, maintaining its relationship with eastern homelands.[1]

Its Tribal Historic Preservation Office leads work with NYC Parks to study and preserve the Kingsbridge battlefield. A National Park Service grant supports surveys that do not disturb the ground, helping reconstruct the fighting and strengthen interpretation.[2]
whereintheworld_content:
The green dot marks the public Chief Nimham Memorial near Van Cortlandt Park East, East 238th Street, and Oneida Avenue, on the park’s eastern edge. Pause at the plaque to read the names and reflect on the soldiers’ service. Follow established park paths and treat this place of remembrance with care.[6]
